abduction: Inference to the best explanation, also called abduction, is a form of reasoning in which you start from surprising facts and work backward to the hypothesis that, if true, would best account for them. Introduced by the American philosopher Charles Peirce, it differs from deduction, which guarantees its conclusion, and induction, which generalizes from examples. Many hold that everyday reasoning, from medical diagnosis to detective work, runs largely on it.
bergson-laughter: For the French philosopher Henri Bergson, comedy has a signature shape: we laugh when something mechanical encrusts itself on the living, as when a person falls like a dropped object, or repeats a fixed gesture when the situation calls for flexibility. In his 1900 essay Laughter, he treats laughter as society's corrective, mocking rigidity back into adaptability. The theory is contested, but many find it captures a familiar comic pattern.
double-consciousness: Double consciousness, coined by W. E. B. Du Bois, describes the divided self-awareness of people forced to see themselves both through their own eyes and through the contemptuous gaze of a dominant society. Du Bois called it a 'two-ness' of being Black and American at once. On this view, the oppressed must measure their self-worth against a degrading mirror, a burden many extend to anyone living between conflicting social worlds.
drowning-child: In Peter Singer's famous thought experiment, you pass a shallow pond where a small child is drowning; wading in will ruin your shoes. Nearly everyone agrees you must help, and Singer draws a provocative conclusion: by similar reasoning, we are obligated to aid distant strangers dying of poverty whenever the cost to us is comparably slight. Critics question whether distance and proximity really make no moral difference.
frankfurt-bullshit: In his 1986 essay On Bullshit, the philosopher Harry Frankfurt distinguished the bullshitter from the liar: a liar knows the truth and deliberately distorts it, while the bullshitter does not care whether what he says is true or false, since his words serve another purpose, like impressing or selling. Bullshit is, on this view, the more corrosive attitude, because indifference to truth erodes the capacity to recognize it.
freud-death-drive: In Freud's later theory, the mind is driven by two opposing forces: Eros, the life drive that binds and preserves, and Thanatos, the death drive that pushes toward aggression, destruction, and ultimately a return to an inorganic state. Introduced in 1920 partly to explain traumatic dreams and compulsive repetition, it remains one of his most speculative and contested ideas, though it continues to shape psychoanalytic, literary, and film interpretation.
freud-unconscious: The unconscious, in Freud's theory, is the vast part of the mind kept outside awareness: desires, memories, and conflicts repressed because they are unacceptable, yet influencing behavior through dreams, slips of the tongue, and symptoms. On this view we are strangers to ourselves, and what we take as free choice often expresses hidden wishes. The theory has been revised, but few doubt that much mental life is unconscious.
golden-rule: The Golden Rule, treat others as you would want to be treated, appears in nearly every major ethical and religious tradition, from Confucius to Jesus, and it captures reciprocity: your treatment of others should survive imagining yourself in their place. Critics note it can misfire when others' wants differ from yours, so many formulate it as asking how others would wish to be treated.
historical-materialism: Historical materialism is Karl Marx's theory of history: the way a society produces its material life, meaning who owns the tools and who does the labor, fundamentally shapes its laws, politics, religion, and ruling ideas. On this view, history advances through class struggle, as changes in economic structures eventually overturn old institutions and ideologies. Critics argue it underplays culture, ideas, and individual agency in shaping how events actually unfold.
hume-is-ought: David Hume observed that writers slide imperceptibly from describing what is the case to prescribing what ought to be, even though no moral conclusion follows from facts alone without an added value premise. This is-ought gap means you cannot establish that something is natural, common, or traditional and thereby prove it right. Many treat the point as logic; how, or whether, the gap can be bridged remains a live debate.
kierkegaard-anxiety: For Kierkegaard, anxiety is not fear of any particular thing but the dizzying awareness of one's own freedom: standing before open possibility, we feel both attraction and dread at being able to choose. He called it the dizziness of freedom, felt by a self that is both finite and infinite. On his account, anxiety is unavoidable and even educative, part of becoming a self.
levinas-face: For Emmanuel Levinas, ethics begins in the face-to-face encounter with another person. The face of the Other, vulnerable and irreducible to any concept, issues a silent command: do not kill me, respond to me. On this view, responsibility for the other person comes before any theory, rule, or calculation, and the self is constituted by answering that call rather than by self-interest.
mackinnon-dominance: Catharine MacKinnon's dominance approach holds that gender inequality runs deeper than laws or attitudes: men's dominance over women, she argues, is built into sexuality itself, and pornography is not merely explicit material but the eroticized subordination of women, a practice that trains desire and entrenches hierarchy. On this view, formal equality can mask continuing powerlessness. Critics contend the approach overstates pornography's effects and risks conflating depiction with endorsement.
natural-kinds: Philosophers distinguish natural kinds from nominal kinds. Natural kinds, like water, gold, or tigers, are held to be genuine divisions in nature, discovered rather than invented, each with an underlying structure explaining why its members share properties. Nominal kinds, like chair or game or zombie, exist only through our classificatory practice. Many hold that nature supplies real differences but never carves itself into kinds, leaving some line-drawing to us.
philosophical-zombies: A philosophical zombie is a hypothetical being physically identical to a human, same brain, same behavior, same words about its feelings, but with no inner experience at all: the lights are on and nobody is home. David Chalmers and others argue such beings are conceivable, suggesting consciousness is something more than physical function. Critics deny the scenario is coherent, which keeps it among philosophy of mind's most disputed puzzles.
plantinga-basic-beliefs: In Reformed epistemology, associated with Alvin Plantinga, a belief is properly basic when rational to hold without supporting arguments, as with belief in other minds or the past. Plantinga argues belief in God can be properly basic too: formed naturally, many hold through an inbuilt sense of the divine, and rational unless defeated by reasons against it. This challenges evidentialism, the demand that every belief rest on evidence.
pythagorean-harmony: The ancient Pythagoreans held that the cosmos is ordered by number: musical consonance follows simple ratios, and they inferred that the planets, moving in similar proportions, must produce a cosmic music, the harmony of the spheres. The music is inaudible to us, on the traditional telling, because we hear it constantly from birth. Though not science, the idea powerfully influenced Western thought linking mathematics, music, and astronomy.
quine-indeterminacy: Willard Van Orman Quine argued that the evidence available to a translator, everything people say and do, underdetermines how their words should be translated: multiple, mutually incompatible manuals of translation could fit all the behavioral facts, with no further fact deciding between them. His gavagai example shows that even pointing cannot fix whether a word means rabbit, undetached rabbit parts, or rabbit stages. Whether such indeterminacy is real remains contested.
schopenhauer-will: For Arthur Schopenhauer, the world's inner reality is Will: a blind, ceaseless striving beneath all appearances, driving nature and human desire alike. Because willing springs from lack, satisfaction is fleeting, and life swings between suffering and boredom, a pessimism he thought music expresses most directly, being a copy of the Will itself. Release, he proposed, comes through art, compassion, and ultimately the ascetic denial of desire.
sense-reference: Gottlob Frege distinguished a name's reference, the actual thing it points to, from its sense, the particular way that thing is presented to thought. The morning star and the evening star refer to the same planet, Venus, yet differ in sense, so someone can know one fact without knowing the other. This distinction remains a cornerstone of the philosophy of language.
spinoza-monism: Baruch Spinoza argued that there is only one substance, God or Nature, of which everything that exists is a mode or aspect. Mind and body, on this view, are not two kinds of stuff but two attributes of one reality, so the universe is a single, self-caused whole unfolding by necessity. His formula God, that is, Nature scandalized contemporaries, and the position is often read as a rigorous pantheism.
sufficient-reason: The principle of sufficient reason, associated especially with Leibniz, states that nothing exists or happens without a reason: for every fact there must be a sufficient explanation of why it is so and not otherwise. Leibniz used it to argue for God as the ultimate explanation of the universe. Critics ask why the principle should hold universally, and whether anything, even the whole cosmos, can have a complete explanation.
thomson-violinist: Judith Jarvis Thomson's 1971 thought experiment asks you to imagine waking attached, without your consent, to an unconscious violinist whose kidneys will fail unless your body sustains him for nine months. Even granting he has a right to life, she argues, this does not give him a right to your body. The argument aimed to show the abortion debate would not be settled even if a fetus were a person.
trolley-problem: The trolley problem, from Philippa Foot and Judith Jarvis Thomson, contrasts cases: a runaway trolley will kill five people unless you divert it onto a track where it kills one, which many permit, yet throwing one person off a bridge to save the same five strikes most as wrong. The puzzle is why our judgments diverge when the arithmetic is identical, and it strains both consequentialist and duty-based ethics.
